title: Diversification
subtitle: Don't put all your eggs in one basket - the oldest rule in investing
openingQuestion: Investor A puts 100% of their capital into one stock. Investor B splits it evenly across 20 stocks in different industries. Who bears more risk if one company suddenly hits a scandal?
openingOptions: Cannot be compared without more information
A - if that single company hits a scandal, A's entire capital is affected; B only feels the impact on 1/20 of the portfolio
B, because more stocks means more complexity
explanation: Diversification is a strategy of spreading capital across many different assets to reduce unsystematic risk - the risk specific to a single company or industry. When one holding runs into trouble, the others aren't affected the same way, protecting the portfolio's total value.

diagram.label: Capital concentrated in a single asset
That asset hits its own specific risk
Spread capital across many different assets

realWorldExample.description: Enron employees put most of their retirement savings into their own company's stock - when Enron collapsed from accounting fraud, thousands of employees lost nearly all of their retirement savings at once, a painful lesson in the cost of not diversifying.

quiz.question: Can diversification completely eliminate every kind of investment risk?
options: No, because trading costs always eat up that entire benefit
Yes, if you hold thirty stocks across different industries
Yes, as long as the assets are negatively correlated with each other
No, the market's systematic risk remains intact
quiz.explanation: Total risk = systematic risk (which cannot be diversified away) + unsystematic risk (which diversification can reduce). When global stock markets collapse (like 2008, 2020), nearly every risky asset drops in price at once - this is systematic risk, unavoidable through diversification.

quiz.question: What distinct benefit does INTERNATIONAL diversification (investing in stocks across many countries, not just diversifying by industry within one country) provide compared to purely domestic diversification?
options: It further reduces macro risk specific to each individual country
It fully and permanently eliminates every currency risk the investor is exposed to
It guarantees a higher return than investing domestically alone
It lowers trading costs by accessing more exchanges
quiz.explanation: International diversification adds a layer of risk reduction beyond industry diversification: country-specific macro risk (monetary policy, the economic cycle, political stability) - though during a global crisis, correlation across international markets can also rise temporarily.

quiz.question: How do systematic risk and unsystematic risk differ?
options: Systematic risk only affects stocks, while unsystematic risk only ever affects bonds and fixed-income instruments
Unsystematic risk can be reduced through diversification, systematic risk cannot
Systematic risk is measured by standard deviation, unsystematic risk by beta
Unsystematic risk only exists at unlisted companies
quiz.explanation: A factory fire is one company's own risk and vanishes once you hold thirty tickers. A recession hits everyone at once - no number of stocks avoids it, and that is exactly the portion of risk the market pays you to bear.

quiz.question: Why does adding the fiftieth stock to a portfolio barely reduce risk any further?
options: Because the trading cost of the fiftieth ticker exceeds the benefit it brings
Because every stock listed in the same domestic market always carries a correlation of exactly one with every other
Because the individual-asset-specific risk has already been mostly diversified away
Because funds are legally capped on the number of tickers they may hold
quiz.explanation: The diversification benefit fades very quickly: most of the individual-asset risk disappears somewhere between twenty and thirty tickers. After that, only market risk remains, and adding tickers doesn't reduce that.

quiz.question: You hold thirty stocks, but all of them are in banking. What's the problem?
options: The portfolio's expected return will be lower than average
There's no problem at all, since thirty different tickers is already more than enough for genuine diversification
Tracking thirty tickers in the same industry is too costly
Industry risk remains intact because all the tickers take the same shock together
quiz.explanation: Diversification is counted by source of risk, not by number of tickers. One interest-rate decision or one wave of bad loans hits all thirty tickers at once, so in terms of risk they're nearly a single investment.

keyTakeaways: Diversification: spreading capital across many assets to reduce unsystematic risk
It cannot eliminate systematic risk (the broad market, macro conditions)
The most basic and oldest investment principle, applying at any portfolio size

practicePrompt.question: An investor buys only one real-estate stock, believing that industry will boom. If real estate hits a crisis, their entire portfolio suffers heavily. What strategy could reduce this kind of risk (the risk specific to one company/industry)?
options: They should put all their capital into a different, higher-potential stock to offset the real-estate stock's risk
Diversification is spreading capital across many assets to reduce unsystematic risk
They should pull all money out of the stock market and hold only cash to avoid every risk
Diversification has no effect at all on the risk specific to one company or industry
practicePrompt.explanation: Diversification: spreading capital across many assets to reduce unsystematic risk (the risk specific to one company/industry). Genuine diversification rests on low correlation between assets, not simply buying many tickers in the same industry.

summary.keyIdea: Diversification: spreading capital across many assets to reduce unsystematic risk
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: It cannot eliminate systematic risk (the broad market, macro conditions)

application.title: Check your own level of diversification
application.message: Look back at your current portfolio - if over 50% of its value sits in a single stock or a single industry, that's a sign you're carrying more unsystematic risk than necessary.
application.secondary: You don't need perfect diversification right away, just an awareness of where your risk is concentrated.

sections.text: Diversification is the oldest and simplest rule in investing: don't put all your eggs in one basket. Technically, it's a strategy of spreading capital across many different assets to reduce unsystematic risk - risk specific to one company or one industry, not risk affecting the whole economy.
Diversification does not erase every risk

An asset's total risk has two parts: systematic risk (interest rates, recessions, global crises - affecting almost every asset at once) and unsystematic risk (a company-specific problem like accounting fraud, a defective product, weak leadership). Diversification only eliminates the second kind. When global markets collapse, as in 2008 or 2020, nearly every risky asset falls in price together - that is systematic risk, and no amount of diversification avoids it.

In 2001, many Enron employees put most of their retirement savings into their own company's stock - both their employer and their only investment. When Enron collapsed from accounting fraud, thousands of people lost nearly all their retirement savings at the same moment they lost their jobs. A painful demonstration of bundling income risk and investment risk into a single source.
International diversification - another layer of protection

Diversifying by industry within one country isn't enough. Investing in stocks across many countries further reduces risk tied to each COUNTRY's own economic cycle, monetary policy, and political instability - markets don't always move in lockstep. That said, during a global crisis, correlation across international markets tends to rise temporarily too.

items: It cannot eliminate systematic risk (the broad market, macro conditions, interest rates)
Don't bundle your income and your investments into the same source (the Enron lesson)
International diversification adds a layer of protection against each country's own macro risk

lines: Diversification doesn't make you risk-free - it just ensures you don't lose everything to a single mistake.
